choices.text: A spontaneous interconversion of two isomers, usually by moving a hydrogen
A way of drawing one compound with its π electrons in different places
choices.why: That describes resonance forms, which are different representations of a single compound.

choices.text: The removal of an α hydrogen by a base to give an anion
choices.why: That is enolate ion formation. Tautomers are neutral isomers that interconvert.

choices.text: An interconversion between two compounds with different molecular formulas
choices.why: Tautomers are isomers, so they have the same molecular formula.

explanation: Tautomerism (from the Greek tauto, "the same," and meros, "part") is the spontaneous interconversion between two isomers, usually with a change in the position of a hydrogen. The keto and enol isomers of a carbonyl compound are tautomers.

prompt: How do tautomers differ from resonance forms?

choices.text: Tautomers are different compounds; resonance forms are drawings of one compound
Tautomers differ only in the positions of their π and nonbonding electrons
choices.why: That describes resonance forms. Tautomers have their atoms, usually a hydrogen, in different places.

choices.text: Resonance forms are constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly
choices.why: Resonance forms aren't isomers at all. They are different drawings of a single compound.

choices.text: They don't differ; keto and enol forms are resonance forms of each other
choices.why: Keto and enol forms are tautomers: different compounds that are constitutional isomers.

explanation: Tautomers are constitutional isomers, different compounds with different structures, while resonance forms are different representations of a single compound. Tautomers have their atoms arranged differently; resonance forms differ only in the position of their π and nonbonding electrons.

choices.text: Acetone, CH3COCH3, and its enol, CH2=C(OH)CH3
Acetone, CH3COCH3, and 2-propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3
choices.why: These have different formulas (C3H6O and C3H8O), so they aren't isomers at all.

choices.text: The two resonance forms of the acetone enolate ion
choices.why: Resonance forms are two drawings of one species, not two different compounds.

choices.text: Acetone, CH3COCH3, and its enolate ion, CH2=C(O−)CH3
choices.why: The enolate ion has one hydrogen fewer and a negative charge, so it isn't an isomer of acetone.

explanation: A carbonyl compound with a hydrogen on its α carbon is in equilibrium with its enol isomer. Acetone and CH2=C(OH)CH3 have the same formula and differ in where one hydrogen is, so they are keto and enol tautomers.

prompt: About how much of its enol tautomer does cyclohexanone contain at room temperature?

choices.text: About 0.0001%
About 76%
choices.why: That is the figure for 2,4-pentanedione, whose enol is stabilized by conjugation and intramolecular hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: About 50%
choices.why: Most monocarbonyl compounds exist almost entirely in their keto form at equilibrium.

choices.text: About 10%
choices.why: Far too high. Cyclohexanone is almost entirely keto; its enol is only about 0.0001%.

explanation: Most monocarbonyl compounds exist almost entirely in their keto form, and it's usually difficult to isolate the pure enol. Cyclohexanone contains only about 0.0001% enol at room temperature, and the percentage is even lower for carboxylic acids, esters, and amides.

prompt: When can the enol tautomer predominate at equilibrium?

choices.text: When it is stabilized by conjugation or intramolecular hydrogen bonding
When the carbonyl compound is a carboxylic acid, an ester, or an amide
choices.why: Carboxylic acids, esters, and amides contain even less enol than ketones such as cyclohexanone.

choices.text: Whenever an acid or base catalyst is present
choices.why: Acids and bases catalyze the interconversion; they don't make the enol the major form.

choices.text: When the compound is a simple ketone such as cyclohexanone
choices.why: Cyclohexanone is only about 0.0001% enol.

explanation: The enol can only predominate when it is stabilized by conjugation or intramolecular hydrogen bonding. Thus, 2,4-pentanedione is about 76% enol. Although enols are usually scarce, they are so reactive that they are responsible for much of the chemistry of carbonyl compounds.

prompt: What is the first step in acid-catalyzed enol formation?

choices.text: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen
Removal of an α hydrogen to give an enolate ion
choices.why: That is the first step of base-catalyzed enol formation.

choices.text: Protonation of the α carbon
choices.why: The acid protonates the oxygen. The cation then loses H+ from the α carbon.

choices.text: Loss of H+ from the carbonyl oxygen
choices.why: The carbonyl oxygen has no hydrogen to lose at the start; it is protonated first.

explanation: In acid catalysis (Figure 22.1.1a), the carbonyl oxygen is first protonated to give an intermediate cation, which then loses H+ from its α carbon to yield the neutral enol.

prompt: In acid-catalyzed enol formation, the cation intermediate loses H+ from its α carbon. Which earlier reaction step does this resemble?

choices.text: A carbocation losing H+ to form an alkene in an E1 reaction
Backside attack by a nucleophile in an S_N2 reaction
choices.why: No nucleophile attacks carbon here; the cation simply loses a proton.

choices.text: A nucleophile adding to a carbocation in an S_N1 reaction
choices.why: The cation loses H+ rather than gaining a nucleophile.

choices.text: Electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene
choices.why: That is an addition. Here a proton is lost and a C=C bond forms.

explanation: The proton loss from the cation intermediate is similar to what happens in an E1 reaction, when a carbocation loses H+ to form an alkene (Section 11.10).

prompt: In base-catalyzed tautomerism, what happens if the enolate ion is protonated on the α carbon?

choices.text: The keto tautomer is regenerated, with no net change
The enol tautomer forms instead of the keto form
choices.why: The enol forms only when the enolate is protonated on oxygen.

choices.text: An α-substituted carbonyl compound forms
choices.why: Adding H+ back to the α carbon just gives back the starting compound.

choices.text: The hydrogen ends up on the β carbon instead
choices.why: The proton goes back on the α carbon. β hydrogens aren't involved, because they aren't acidic.

explanation: Base removes an α hydrogen to give a resonance-stabilized enolate ion, which is then protonated. Protonation on the α carbon regenerates the keto tautomer with no net change; protonation on oxygen gives the enol (Figure 22.1.1b).

prompt: Why can a base remove the α hydrogens of a carbonyl compound but not its β, γ, or δ hydrogens?

choices.text: Only the anion from removing an α hydrogen is resonance-stabilized by the carbonyl
The β, γ, and δ carbons are more electronegative than the α carbon
choices.why: They are all carbon atoms. The difference is whether the anion formed can be resonance-stabilized by the carbonyl group.

choices.text: β, γ, and δ hydrogens are too far from the base to be reached
choices.why: The base can reach them; the anions that would result just aren't stabilized by the carbonyl group.

choices.text: α hydrogens are the only hydrogens bonded to carbon
choices.why: β, γ, and δ hydrogens are also bonded to carbon.

explanation: Only the hydrogens on the α position of a carbonyl compound are acidic. Hydrogens at β, γ, δ, and so on can't be removed by base because the resulting anions can't be resonance-stabilized by the carbonyl group.

prompt: What is the enol tautomer of propanal, CH3CH2CHO?

choices.text: CH3CH=CHOH
CH2=CHCH2OH
choices.why: Here the –OH isn't on a carbon of the C=C bond, so this isn't an enol. In the enol, the C=C joins the α carbon and the former carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: CH2=C(OH)CH3
choices.why: That is the enol of acetone, which has a different carbon skeleton from propanal.

choices.text: CH3CH2CH2OH
choices.why: That is 1-propanol, which has two more hydrogens. Tautomers are isomers with the same formula.

explanation: To form the enol, a hydrogen moves from the α carbon (the CH2 next to the carbonyl) to the oxygen, and the C=C forms between the α carbon and the former carbonyl carbon: CH3CH=CHOH.

prompt: 2,4-Pentanedione is about 76% enol tautomer at equilibrium. About what percentage is in the keto form?
explanation: 100% − 76% = 24% keto. 2,4-Pentanedione is unusual: its enol is stabilized by conjugation and intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so the enol predominates.

prompt: How many acidic hydrogens does cyclopentanone have?
explanation: Cyclopentanone has two α carbons, one on each side of the carbonyl group, and each is a CH2. That gives 2 × 2 = 4 acidic α hydrogens (Exercise 22.1.2). The other ring hydrogens are β and aren't acidic.

prompt: How many acidic α hydrogens does phenylacetone, C6H5CH2COCH3, have?
explanation: Both carbons next to the carbonyl are α carbons: the CH2 has 2 hydrogens and the CH3 has 3, for 5 in all (Exercise 22.1.2). The benzene-ring hydrogens are not on an α carbon.

prompt: How many acidic hydrogens does ethyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH3, have?
explanation: Only the CH3 attached to the carbonyl carbon is an α carbon, so ethyl acetate has 3 acidic hydrogens (Exercise 22.1.2). The OCH2CH3 hydrogens are on the other side of the oxygen and aren't α to the carbonyl.

prompt: How many acidic α hydrogens does 2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH3)3CCHO, have?
explanation: The α carbon is bonded to three CH3 groups and carries no hydrogen. The nine CH3 hydrogens are β and aren't acidic, and the aldehyde hydrogen is on the carbonyl carbon, not the α carbon (compare propanal, with 2 acidic hydrogens, in Exercise 22.1.2). So this aldehyde has 0 acidic hydrogens and has no enol tautomer.
